newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil CVRD sale threatened by legal battles.
newsitem.headline: Brazil CVRD sale threatened by legal battles.

text.p: Brazil Monday conceded the planned auction of mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) might be nudged off-track by law suits but vowed its lawyers would work all night to ensure the sale went ahead.
Jose Pio Borges, privatisation chief of the National Development Bank said a record 103 court challenges to the privatisation had been lodged and nine injunctions had been granted by late afternoon.
"The auction is suspended due to court decisions," he said in Rio de Janeiro, where 45 percent of CVRD's voting shares were due to go under the hammer Tuesday morning.

In the capital Brasilia, National Development Bank head Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros acknowledged everything depended on the courts and said a small army of government lawyers would keep on working till late Tuesday afternoon to have the injunctions overturned.
"If it's not possible (to overturn the injunctions by Tuesday afternoon) we will have to carry out a postponement," Mendonca de Barros said.

The privatisation of CVRD, the world's largest iron ore exporter, should raise at least $5 billion for the government's coffers once completed and thus qualify as the biggest Latin American state sell-off to date.

CVRD's Carajas mine, deep in the Amazon, holds the world's largest iron ore deposit estimated at 18 billion metric tons. The group, which enjoys a rare public sector reputation for efficiency, also mines copper, gold and manganese.
The controlling stake that was to be offered Tuesday is valued at $2.8 billion, with two multinational consortia in the bidding.
Brasilia enjoyed two legal victories Monday when the country's highest court, The Supreme Federal Tribunal, rejected two challenges to the CVRD sell-off.
But judicial officials acknowledged they were concerned after a Sao Paulo judge rejected a government appeal against one of the many injunctions handed out by regional courts.
"We are concerned about the possibility of last-minute injunctions and fear the chances of the auction going ahead without hitch are diminishing," a high-ranking source said.

Opponents of the privatisation, ranging from former presidents Jose Sarney and Itamar Franco to all of the country's Catholic bishops, have called for a giant demonstration outside the Rio stock exchange on Tuesday.
Officials said 600 riot police would protect the bolsa. The square in front of the exchange was fenced off on Monday.
Marcelo Sereno, first secretary of Latin America's largest trade union confederation, the CUT, said he expected 5,000 people to turn up.
"It'll be huge," he said at a smaller protest held Monday outside National Development Bank headquarters in Rio.
The protest is also likely to turn violent, Sereno said.
On Sunday, some 200 demonstrators booing Cardoso as he ended his meeting with Menem were by forcefully dispersed police firing tear gas grenades and wading into the crowd with batons.
